q: Why does a database fetch a whole page when an index has already located the row?
options: Disks serve whole blocks rather than single bytes, and the row's position within the page is stored in the page itself
Reading a whole page lets the database skip the checksum, which would otherwise be computed for every row
Rows are compressed as a group, so one row can't be decoded without its neighbours on the page
The operating system refuses reads smaller than 8 KB, which is why Postgres chose that page size
why: Block devices aren't byte addressable, and row sizes vary, so only the page can be computed. Neighbouring rows arrive for free, which helps range reads.

q: To read pages 2 through 9 of a table with 8 KB pages, what does the database ask the OS for?
options: Offset 16,384 and length 65,536 in the table's file
Offset 16,484 and length 65,536 in the table's file
Offset 8,192 and length 57,344 in the table's file
Eight separate reads, because pages can't be requested together
why: Offset is page number times page size: 2 × 8192 = 16,384. Eight pages are 65,536 bytes. No lookup is needed because every page is the same size.

q: What does the ctid (2,5) mean in Postgres?
options: Page 2, line pointer 5, which holds the row's offset and length within that page
Byte offset 2,005 in the table's file, counted from the first row
Transaction 2 created this row, and it's the fifth version of it
Partition 2, row 5 of that partition's sorted order
why: A ctid is (page, line pointer). The pointer gives the indirection that lets a row move inside its page without changing its address.

q: You run UPDATE on one row, then read the page with pageinspect. What do you find?
options: A new row version with its own line pointer, and the old version still there with xmax set
The same line pointer with the new value overwritten in place, and a note in the WAL
The old row removed and its space reused by the new version straight away
The new version on the next page, because updates always move rows to a fresh page
why: Postgres never overwrites a row. The old version stays for older snapshots, and only VACUUM reclaims it.

q: A heap page has special = 8192 and a B-tree page has special = 8176. What does that tell you?
options: Heap pages have no special space, while the index page reserves 16 bytes for index data such as sibling links
The index page is 16 bytes smaller than a heap page, because indexes use a shorter page size
Both have a special space, but the heap's is at the very start of the page
The index page has 16 free bytes left, so it's about to split
why: special marks where the special space starts. For a table it equals the page size, meaning there's none. Index pages keep access-method data there.

q: The course repeats a criticism that 1,000 items would spend half an 8 KB page on line pointers. What did measuring show?
options: A heap page can't hold 1,000 rows: the smallest rows fit about 226, so pointers took about 11% of the page
It's correct: at 1,000 rows, 4 KB of the page is line pointers
Pointers are stored on a separate page, so they take no room in the data page at all
Line pointers are only 1 byte each, so even 1,000 of them use a tiny share
why: Each row has a tuple header, so rows can't be that small. 226 rows × 4 bytes of pointers is about 900 bytes of the page.

q: A row holds a 1.7 MB text value, yet the main table stays at one 8 KB page. Why?
options: TOAST compressed the value and moved it out of line, since a row can't span pages
Postgres truncates values longer than a page and keeps the rest in the WAL
The value is stored as a chain of rows across many pages of the same table
Large text columns are kept in the buffer pool only and never reach the table's file
why: Past about 2 KB, TOAST compresses and moves large values to a side table. The docs state that tuples can't span pages.

q: Insert ids 3, 1, 2 and select with no ORDER BY. What do Postgres and InnoDB return, and why?
options: Postgres gives 3, 1, 2 because a heap has no order, and InnoDB gives 1, 2, 3 because rows live in the primary key's tree
Both give 1, 2, 3, because a primary key always sorts the table
Both give 3, 1, 2, because rows are always returned in insertion order
Postgres gives 1, 2, 3 because of its primary key index, and InnoDB gives 3, 1, 2 from its heap
why: That's the heap and clustered difference. Neither order is a promise: only ORDER BY guarantees one.

q: An index on email only. MySQL answers SELECT id ... WHERE email = ? with 'Using index', but Postgres visits the table. Why?
options: InnoDB's secondary index entries contain the primary key, so id is already there
MySQL caches primary keys in memory, while Postgres has to read them from disk
Postgres can't do index-only scans on text columns
InnoDB rewrites the query to use the primary key index instead of the email index
why: A Postgres index entry holds the key and a heap address, so id needs the heap, unless you add it with INCLUDE.

q: Why is a column store slow at updating a single row?
options: Each column lives in its own pages, so one row touches a page per column, often in compressed blocks
Column stores don't support UPDATE, so an update is always a full table rewrite
Every row in a column store has to be re-sorted whenever any value changes
Column stores keep no primary key, so finding the row needs a full scan of every column
why: The layout that makes reading one column cheap makes writing one row expensive. Row stores write the row in one place.

q: Which statement about a plain secondary index in Oracle is right?
options: By default it stores a rowid, and storing the primary key only applies to index-organized tables
It always stores the primary key, exactly as InnoDB does
It stores the whole row, so Oracle never needs to read the table
It stores a hash of the row rather than an address
why: My notes said MySQL and Oracle both store the primary key. That's true of InnoDB and of Oracle's IOTs, while Oracle's default heap tables use rowids.

q: A SELECT shows Buffers: shared hit=934. What does that mean?
options: 934 pages were touched, all found in the buffer pool, so no disk read was needed but the work still happened
934 rows were returned to the client from cached results
934 milliseconds were spent waiting on shared locks
934 pages were written back to disk during the query
why: Buffers count pages. hit means already in memory, read means fetched from outside the buffer pool. A hit still costs CPU.

q: What does an SSD do when a page has to be rewritten?
options: Writes to a fresh page and remaps the logical block, leaving the old page to be erased later
Overwrites the same cells in place, which is what wears out that exact spot
Erases the whole drive region first, then writes the page back
Keeps the change in RAM until the block has 100 changes, then rewrites it once
why: Flash can't overwrite a page. The controller remaps and spreads wear, so the real concern is write amplification, not one hot spot dying.

q: A plan shows Sort (cost=136537.84..139037.84). What do those numbers mean?
options: Estimated cost in arbitrary units: before the first row, then for all rows
Milliseconds: the fastest and slowest run of this node
Bytes of memory the sort used, before and after spilling
Rows sorted so far, and rows still waiting
why: A sort must read everything before output, so its startup cost is nearly its total. Cost isn't time: only actual time is in milliseconds.

q: Why can a Bitmap Heap Scan beat an Index Scan on the same index?
options: It notes which pages hold matches first, then reads each page once in order, instead of jumping per row
It stores a copy of the rows in the bitmap, so it never reads the table
It avoids the index altogether by using the table's statistics
It reads rows in random order, which spreads the load across the disk
why: An Index Scan follows pointers one at a time, and may revisit pages. A bitmap turns that into one sorted pass, and needs a recheck because a page holds other rows.

q: In the measured sweep, what happened to a forced Index Scan as the matching share of a random column approached 100%?
options: It reached 428 ms, while a Seq Scan took 56 ms, because each row cost a random page jump
It stayed the fastest plan throughout, since the index was in memory
It became identical to the Seq Scan, because Postgres converts it automatically
It stopped working, and Postgres raised an error about too many index reads
why: A Seq Scan reads each page once. An Index Scan on a randomly ordered column jumps around for every row, a million times.

q: You index g, and a query on a range of g gets slower than with no index. What's the likely reason?
options: Matches are on nearly every page, so the table is read anyway, plus the index, and parallelism is lost
The index was built concurrently, so it isn't usable for ranges
Indexes only help equality, so a range always makes things worse
The planner stops using statistics once an index exists
why: In the run, the bitmap visited 24,340 pages and spilled its sort. Only a covering index, which avoided the table, cut the pages read.

q: EXPLAIN says Index Only Scan, but it's slow and Heap Fetches is 49,999. What's the fix?
options: Run VACUUM, so the visibility map marks those pages all-visible
Drop and rebuild the index, because Heap Fetches means it's corrupted
Add the column to the index with INCLUDE
Raise work_mem so that the heap fits in memory
why: An index doesn't know row visibility. If a page's bit isn't set, the scan must check the heap. VACUUM sets the bits, and writes clear them.

q: What's the difference between key and non-key columns in CREATE INDEX i ON t (id) INCLUDE (name)?
options: id is sorted and searchable, and name is only carried in the leaf pages to allow index-only scans
Both are sorted, but name comes second, so it only helps range queries
name is hashed for fast equality search, while id is kept as a B-tree
name is stored in the table only, and the index just remembers its offset
why: Non-key columns can't be searched. They make the index bigger, so include them only when you know the query needs them.

q: On Postgres 18, a composite index on (a, b) served WHERE b = 40, with Index Searches: 103. How?
options: A skip scan: the index is searched once per distinct value of a, which works when a has few values
Postgres 18 stores a second copy of the index sorted by b
The planner reversed the column order and rebuilt the index for this query
The filter ran on the table, and the index was only used to count rows
why: The old rule said b alone couldn't use it. With a million distinct values of a, the same query still fell back to a Seq Scan.

q: WHERE x + 1 = 501 doesn't use the index on x, though WHERE x = 500 does. Why?
options: The index stores x, not x + 1, so the planner can't match the expression to it
Arithmetic in a WHERE clause disables all indexes for the whole query
The planner evaluates x + 1 only after the index scan finishes
Index lookups only work when the column is on the right-hand side
why: Rewrite the condition, or create an index on the expression itself.

q: WHERE state = 'California' does a Seq Scan, and WHERE state = 'Florida' uses the index on the same column. Why?
options: Statistics show California covers almost every row, so an index would only add work, while Florida is rare
The index only stores values that appear fewer than 100 times
Postgres alternates between plans to spread the load
The first query warmed the cache, so the planner picked an index for the second
why: Selectivity depends on the value, not only the column. Same index, opposite plans.

q: A plan's estimate is rows=1, and the actual count is 999,990. What's the most likely cause?
options: Stale statistics: ANALYZE hasn't run since a bulk load
The index is corrupted and must be rebuilt
A parallel worker lost part of its count
The table has too many partitions to estimate
why: The planner works from statistics. Comparing estimated and actual rows is the first thing to check. After ANALYZE, the plan changed.

q: What does `Index Searches: 3` against `Index Searches: 1` show for IN (1, 5003, 9000) and BETWEEN 1 AND 9000?
options: Three separate descents of the tree, against one descent followed by a walk along the leaves
Three indexes were used, against one index
The first query was retried twice after a lock conflict
The query ran on three parallel workers, against one
why: That's seek against scan. Far-apart values favour separate seeks, and close ones favour one seek plus a walk. Postgres 18 shows the count directly.

q: An index on a column with 10 distinct values across a million rows came out at 6.8 MB, or 21 MB with one option off. Which option?
options: deduplicate_items, which stores each value once followed by a list of row addresses
fillfactor, which leaves empty space in every page
INCLUDE, which copies extra columns into the leaves
CONCURRENTLY, which builds the index in two passes
why: Deduplication arrived in Postgres 13. Without it, a low-cardinality index is as big as one on unique values.

q: What goes wrong with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY if duplicates exist?
options: It fails and leaves an INVALID index behind, which slows writes until you drop it
It silently removes the duplicates to make the index valid
It succeeds, and rejects the duplicates only on the next VACUUM
It rolls everything back automatically, so nothing remains
why: A concurrent build can't run in one transaction, so a failure leaves its catalog entry. \d shows it marked INVALID.

q: A Bloom filter says a name is 'definitely not' present. What makes that answer safe?
options: A clear bit proves the name was never added, as long as every write went through the filter
The filter also keeps a sorted list of names, which it checks first
It's only an estimate, so you still need to query the database
It queries a replica in the background before answering
why: There are no false negatives. A set bit only means maybe, because another name may have set it.

q: What's the effect of adding many more names to a fixed-size Bloom filter?
options: Bits fill up until nearly every answer is 'maybe', so the filter saves nothing
It starts giving false negatives for the oldest names
It automatically grows and rehashes, so nothing changes
It raises an error once half the bits are set
why: That's saturation. It isn't harmful, just useless: you're back to querying every time.

q: Why can't you simply delete a name from a basic Bloom filter?
options: Clearing its bits might erase other names that share them, creating false negatives
Bits can only be written once, because they're stored in read-only memory
Deleting requires knowing every hash function's secret key
A filter is stored compressed, so individual bits can't be reached
why: Sharing bits is what keeps the filter small. To remove items, rebuild it or use a counting variant.

q: Each new follower took 375 ms and 3.6 MB of WAL with a JSON list at a million followers. Why so much?
options: An UPDATE writes a whole new row version, so appending one id rewrites the entire list
JSON columns are stored outside the table, and each read takes a network hop
Postgres re-validates every element of a JSON array against a schema on each write
The follows table index had to be rebuilt on every update
why: MVCC copies the row. A separate follows table stayed at about 3 ms, whatever the account's size.

q: Which is the right order for dealing with a table heading for a billion rows?
options: Avoid it by design, index, partition, shard, and only then brute force
Shard first, since it's the only thing that scales, then partition and index
Brute force first because it needs no changes, then index
Partition, then avoid it, then index, then shard
why: Each rung adds complexity. Brute force suits analytics only, since live rows change while you scan them.

q: In the insert race, InnoDB with random 16-byte keys fell from about 120,000 to about 3,500 rows a second. When?
options: Once the table outgrew the 128 MB buffer pool, so nearly every insert needed a page from disk
As soon as the second batch started, because of lock contention between batches
When autovacuum started rewriting the table in the background
When the key column reached its maximum length
why: Random keys need any page at any time. While the tree fits in memory that's mildly wasteful. After that, inserts thrash.

q: After the race on Postgres, the UUIDv4 index was about 69% full and the UUIDv7 index about 90%. Why?
options: Random keys split pages in the middle and leave them part-empty, while ordered keys only add at the right edge
UUIDv7 values are shorter, so more of them fit in a page
Postgres compresses ordered values, but not random ones
UUIDv4 indexes reserve free space for later updates
why: Same data, emptier pages, so a bigger index: 118 MB against 90 MB, plus more WAL.

q: Why do UUIDv7 and ULID insert like sequential ids?
options: They start with a 48-bit timestamp, so new values sort after older ones
They're generated by a central sequence on the database server
They're shorter than UUIDv4, so they fit at the end of each page
Databases recognise them and store them in a separate ordered file
why: Time first means new keys land at the end of the index, and any client can generate one without coordination.

q: Why does a URL shortener benefit less from ordered keys than Shopify's idempotency keys?
options: Its reads are random whatever the key, while idempotency keys are looked up soon after being written
Short URLs are too short to hold a timestamp
URL shorteners never use B-tree indexes
Ordered keys make writes slower when the table is small
why: Ordered keys always help writes. They help reads only if reads cluster around recent inserts.

q: Two requests with the same idempotency key arrive at once. What does the second INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING do?
options: It waits for the first to finish, then inserts nothing if the first committed
It inserts a second row and leaves cleanup to a background job
It fails at once with a unique violation, before the first commits
It returns the first request's row before that request commits
why: The outcome depends on the first transaction, so the second waits. The customer is charged once.

q: What's a privacy cost of UUIDv7 compared with UUIDv4?
options: Anyone with the id can read when it was created
It reveals the MAC address of the machine that made it
It contains the row's primary key in plain text
It can be reversed to find the client's IP address
why: The timestamp is the first 48 bits. Leaking a MAC address was UUIDv1's problem.

q: Why is the InnoDB slowdown from random keys worse than the Postgres one in these tests?
options: The whole table lives in the primary key's tree, so random keys scatter full rows, not only index entries
InnoDB doesn't have a buffer pool, so each insert goes straight to disk
Postgres sorts random keys before inserting them
InnoDB fsyncs every page of the table on each commit
why: A Postgres heap appends rows, so only the smaller index scatters. It also fit in memory in this test.

q: In a B+Tree, what do internal pages hold?
options: Keys and child pointers only, so that many more fit per page
Keys, values and child pointers, like every other page
Only pointers to the leaves, with no keys at all
Full copies of the rows, for faster reads
why: Values live only in leaves. That raises the fanout, so the tree is shorter and the internal pages stay in memory.

q: Why is a range scan slow on a plain B-Tree?
options: Adjacent keys can sit on different levels, so the scan climbs back through parents and re-reads pages
B-Trees don't keep keys in sorted order
A B-Tree can only be searched for exact matches
Each key has to be looked up from the root in a separate transaction
why: The B+Tree fixes this with linked leaves, so a range becomes a walk along one level.

q: A real Postgres index on a million ints had a root of 10 entries, internal pages of 286, and leaves of 367. How tall was it?
options: Three levels: 10 × 286 × 367 is about a million
Twenty levels, which is log base 2 of a million
Two levels, since 367 × 367 is more than enough
Six levels, one for each digit of a million
why: Fanout multiplies at every level, so real trees are very flat. A fourth level reaches hundreds of millions.

q: Why did int and bigint keys give an index of exactly the same size?
options: Index entries are padded to 8-byte boundaries, so a 4-byte key saves nothing
Postgres stores every integer as 8 bytes internally
Both were deduplicated down to the same size
The index only stores the first 4 bytes of a bigint
why: Both gave 367 entries a leaf and 21 MB. Don't pick int only to shrink an index.

q: The same email index doubled from 18.6 MB to 36.7 MB. What changed?
options: The InnoDB primary key went from an int to a 36-character string, which every secondary entry contains
The emails got longer in the second table
The index was rebuilt with a lower fill factor
The second table used a heap instead of a clustered index
why: Every secondary index entry carries the primary key. A wide key pays again in each index.

q: A B-Tree of degree 5 can hold how many elements in a node?
options: 4: a node with M children holds M − 1 elements
5: one element per child
6: one more element than it has children
It depends only on the page size, so degree doesn't apply
why: The elements separate the children, so there's always one fewer.

q: Where does a B+Tree store a key that's also used to route searches?
options: In an internal page to route, and again in a leaf with its value
Only in the internal page, with the value alongside it
Only in the leaf, with the internal page storing a hash of it
In the root page only, since that's where every search starts
why: That duplication is the small price of keeping all values in the leaves. At an equal key a search goes right.

q: What makes a B-Tree stay balanced?
options: It grows at the top: full pages split upwards, and only a root split adds a level
A background process rebalances the tree every night
New keys are always added to the shortest branch
The tree is rebuilt whenever it becomes uneven
why: Every leaf stays the same distance from the root, so there's no unlucky key.

q: Postgres leaf entries hold a heap address, and InnoDB secondary entries hold a primary key. What's the trade?
options: Postgres reads directly but rows moving can touch every index, while InnoDB moves rows freely but pays a second tree walk
Postgres uses less disk, and InnoDB uses less memory, but they behave the same on updates
InnoDB's approach is always faster for reads, because a key is smaller than an address
Postgres can't have secondary indexes on tables with a primary key
why: This is the root of the Uber story in post 14: update cost against read cost.

q: A range of 5,001 consecutive ids touched only 18 pages. Why so few?
options: One descent of the tree, then a walk along about 14 leaf pages holding hundreds of entries each
The result was already cached, so only 18 pages were needed for the metadata
Each page holds 5,001 entries, and the other pages were skipped
The planner sampled the range rather than reading all of it
why: Index Searches: 1 confirms one descent. Linked leaves turn the rest into a sideways walk.

q: Which is true of Postgres B-tree levels, according to its docs?
options: Each level can be used as a doubly linked list of pages, not only the leaves
Only leaf pages are linked, and only in one direction
No pages are linked: all navigation goes through the root
Pages are linked through the WAL rather than through the page itself
why: The real leaf in the walk showed both neighbours. The docs extend that to every level.

q: A text UUID key fits 141 entries a leaf where an int fits 367, yet both trees were 3 levels high. So what did the wider key cost?
options: Memory: the index was 56 MB instead of 21 MB, competing for the buffer pool
Nothing: if the height is the same, the cost is the same
Lookup speed: each lookup read about 2.6 times as many pages
Correctness: text keys can return rows in the wrong order
why: A lookup still reads 3 pages, but a larger index needs more memory to stay cached. Post 4's cliff shows why that matters.
